title: OmouAI: Argumentative Human-AI Policy Deliberation with Simulated Personas
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 25 Sep 2026]
    Title:OmouAI: Argumentative Human-AI Policy Deliberation with Simulated Personas
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Debates amongst agents driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated vast potential in various applications, but when these interactions include humans and take place in high-stakes environments, e.g., in public policy deliberations, they are beset with issues such as sycophancy and a lack of faithful explanations. To tackle these issues, we present OmouAI, an interactive and inclusive deliberation system that uses LLMs in combination with computational argumentation, a field which excels in representing and reasoning within debates. OmouAI allows a human user to deliberate policy claims for real-world challenges with simulated personas, e.g., representing stakeholders, domain experts or devil's advocates, towards reducing sycophancy. Each persona generates its own arguments, and the arguments of all parties form a shared argumentation framework. Users can then contest, add and revise arguments, providing crucial human oversight. Then, arguments are evaluated using deterministic argumentative semantics against external goals, such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals, guaranteeing faithful explanations. The advancement or worsening of the goals thus serve as indicators for the policy recommendations.

report.summary: OmouAI combines LLMs with computational argumentation so humans can debate policy with simulated personas, curbing sycophancy and grounding recommendations in deterministic, goal-based explanations.
report.background: LLM-driven multi-agent debates have shown promise for reasoning and collective problem-solving, but when humans join high-stakes discussions such as public policy deliberation, two flaws surface: sycophancy, where models flatter or defer to users instead of challenging them, and unfaithful explanations, where the stated rationale does not match the actual decision process. Computational argumentation, a mature field built on formal structures like Dung's frameworks and ASPIC+, excels at representing conflicting claims and evaluating them under explicit semantics. OmouAI bridges these worlds: it uses LLMs to generate arguments from simulated stakeholders, experts and devil's advocates, arranges them in a shared argumentation graph, and then applies deterministic argumentative semantics against external objectives such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals. This mirrors a broader trend toward neuro-symbolic hybrids for trustworthy, auditable AI in governance and civic tech.
key_points: Simulated personas as debate partners: each AI persona, whether a stakeholder, domain expert or devil's advocate, generates its own arguments independently. Because no single model is asked to agree with the user, the design directly targets sycophancy, the tendency of LLMs to flatter and conform rather than push back on weak policy claims.

A shared, editable argumentation framework: all arguments from humans and personas are collected into one structured graph. Users can contest, add or revise arguments at any point, preserving human oversight and making the deliberation inclusive rather than a black-box AI verdict.

Deterministic evaluation against external goals: instead of asking an LLM to judge the debate, OmouAI applies formal argumentative semantics against goals like the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Whether a goal advances or worsens becomes the indicator for the policy recommendation, which the authors argue guarantees faithful explanations.

Addresses two barriers to high-stakes AI use: sycophancy and unfaithful explanations are persistent obstacles to deploying LLMs in policy, law and governance. By separating LLM-based argument generation from rule-based evaluation, the system offers a template for auditable AI-assisted decision-making.

Interactive and inclusive by design: OmouAI is framed as a deliberation system for real-world challenges, not a benchmark. It emphasizes participation, revision and transparency, positioning AI as a facilitator of structured debate rather than an oracle that issues final policy answers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, OmouAI signals that neuro-symbolic hybrids, pairing LLM generation with formal reasoning, can make high-stakes AI more auditable, a direction regulators increasingly demand under frameworks like the EU AI Act. For developers, the key lesson is architectural: let models generate arguments but let deterministic semantics evaluate them, and treat personas as a way to counteract sycophancy rather than a gimmick. Argumentation graphs also offer an inspectable data structure for multi-agent systems. For regular users, this points toward civic and consulting tools that present structured debate instead of a single confident chatbot answer, letting citizens see who argued what, contest claims, and trace recommendations back to explicit goals such as sustainability targets.
report.tools: To explore this space, look at argumentation libraries such as TweetyProject (Java), PyArg and Argdown for building and evaluating argument graphs, plus formal semantics like Dung frameworks and ASPIC+. For LLM debate and persona orchestration, AutoGen, CAMEL and ChatEval are common starting points. On the civic side, Polis and Remesh show real-world deliberation interfaces, while DeepMind's Habermas Machine illustrates AI-mediated consensus. The OmouAI paper itself is the primary reference.
